summary: Reports on a meeting held at an IETF gathering in Houston in November 1993 about the future of white pages directory services for the Internet. It records the discussion and the approaches considered. It is a meeting report, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1588 records a meeting about finding people in a shared Internet directory. It lists what such a directory must do, compares the systems that could do it, and sets out what the meeting recommended.

subtitle: A meeting report on Internet directory services for finding people, and how to make them work.

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a shared directory that helps people find contact information for other users, and X.500 directory services had been slow to deploy because the software was hard to install and nobody managed the system as a whole.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC reports on a November 1993 IETF meeting in Houston organised around four questions: what functions a white pages service must perform, what approaches could provide it, what problems had to be overcome, and what deployment strategy would work.
tldr.outcome: The meeting recommended a common ground approach: many client and server types joined by an interoperation protocol, X.500 kept as a core, simpler services such as Whois++ alongside it, index servers for fast search, and central management of the X.500 system.

facts.label: Netfind scale reported
facts.value: 25k queries per day, users in 4875 domains in 54 countries

facts.label: A Whois++ server in one test

today: RFC 1588 is an Informational meeting report, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records what was said at a November 1993 meeting and defines no protocol of its own.

sections.title: The Meeting and Its Four Questions
sections.content:
This report describes the results of a meeting held at the November IETF in Houston, Texas, on November 2, 1993, to discuss the future of and approaches to a white pages directory service for the Internet. USC/Information Sciences Institute conducted the meeting, as proposed to the National Science Foundation, to discuss the viability of the X.500 directory as a practical approach to providing white pages service in the near future and to identify and discuss any alternatives. An electronic mail mailing list was organised, and discussions were held by email for two weeks before the meeting.

The report is organised around four questions. What functions should a white pages directory perform? What approaches will provide one? What are the problems to be overcome? And what should the deployment strategy be? The report answers each of them in turn, and ends with a short summary and a list of recommendations.

Section 2 gives the background. A meeting on Internet white pages service was initiated by the FRICC in February 1989, and the ensuing discussions produced RFC 1107, which offered some technical conclusions, with widespread deployment expected by mid-1992. Several other RFCs have suggested deployment strategies for an X.500 directory service, and a working draft by A. Jurg of SURFnet describes why a global white pages service is needed. The report notes that deployment of an X.500 directory service, including the PSI White Pages Pilot and the PARADISE project, is significant and continues to grow, albeit at a slower rate than the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The meeting was about how to build a shared list of people that anyone on the Internet could search. The report is organised as four questions and four answers.

sections.title: What a White Pages Service Must Do
sections.content:
The basic function of a white pages service is to find people and information about people. Two functions are required. Searching is the ability to find people given some fuzzy information about them, such as finding the Postel in southern California; a search may often return a list of matches. Retrieval is obtaining additional information associated with a person, such as an address, telephone number, email mailbox, or security certificate.

The report says the recognition of the importance of indexing is a major conclusion of the discussions. Users want fast searching across the distributed database on attributes different from the database structure, and pre-computed indices can satisfy that desire, though only for specified searches. It notes that the idea of indexing is not new, citing the IN-ADDR tree in the Domain Name System as an example.

Security certificates are the third kind of information a directory holds, and they are essential for end-to-end authentication, integrity and privacy in Internet applications. The report says the development of secure applications depends on a directory system for retrieving the certificate associated with an individual, and that the privacy enhanced electronic mail system has been developed and is ready to go into service, but is now hindered by the lack of an easily used directory of security certificates. An open question is whether such a directory needs to be internally secure.

Beyond those two functions, the report lists what a white pages directory should be. It should be flexible, have low resource requirements and fit into other systems in use. It should not cost much, so that future transitions are not too costly, and there should be the ability to migrate to something else if a better solution appears. Local directory information should be shareable with the Internet in a seamless fashion and with little extra effort, and query responses should be reliable and consistent enough that automated tools could use them. RFC 1107 had listed eight requirements of a white pages service, from functionality and correctness of information to size, usage and query rate, response time, partitioned authority, access control and multiple transport protocol support, plus four further features that would make it more useful, including descriptive naming that could support a yellow pages service, accountability, multiple interfaces and multiple clients.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory has two jobs: find a person from vague details, and then show the contact details. It also has to hold the certificates that prove who someone is, and it has to be fast enough that people use it.

sections.title: The Technologies Considered
sections.content:
Section 4 reviews the systems available for finding information. X.500 is the international standard. In its favour are its flexibility, distributed architecture, security, superiority to paper directories, and the fact that it can be used by applications as well as by humans. It is designed to provide a uniform database facility with replication, modification and authorization, and because it is distributed it suits a large global directory. In practice, the report says, X.500 is difficult, too complicated and inconvenient to use.

The report gives three reasons deployment has been slow, which are largely the same reasons people dislike it. The available implementations, mostly quipu based on the ISODE, are very large and complicated packages that solve the general X.500 problem rather than the subset an Internet white pages directory needs. You have to know a lot to get a directory service running with X.500: about object classes and attributes, about getting a distinguished name and an internal tree structure. And getting data to populate the directory, converting it into the right form and keeping it up to date turns out to be a hard problem, which the report notes exists regardless of the protocol used.

Whois++ is simpler. In less than fifteen months after the first discussions in July 1992 there were three working public domain implementations, at least three more on the way and a front-end to X.500. Search is built in, the protocols are simple enough that someone can write a server in three days, and people have done it. A typical implementation is about 10 megabytes including the WAIS source code, and in one test the total for a Whois++ server came to 22 megabytes. The report is careful to say Whois++ is not yet a fully functional white pages service and that work is needed on replication and authentication of data.

Netfind works in two stages: find out where to ask, then start asking. The first stage uses a database of netnews articles, UUCP maps, NIC WHOIS databases and DNS traversals; the second uses finger queries, WHOIS queries, SMTP expns and vrfys, and DNS lookups. Its key feature is that it is proactive: the system administrator does not have to bring up a server or populate it. The report gives its scale as 25k queries per day and users in 4875 domains in 54 countries, and notes that the legality of proactive methods is in question in some countries. Archie succeeds for the same reason, gathering data with the same mechanism used to transfer the files, so the success rate is near 100 percent. The report notes the difference: for white pages, tools were being built but there was no data. Finger can check that a particular person has an account on a particular host, but is not an efficient way to search. Gateways exist between Gopher and X.500 and beginnings of one between WWW and X.500, and the report proposes a WWW URI or URL attribute type in the directory so that a client can ask for either the locator or the data itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Several directory systems existed. X.500 was powerful but hard to set up and use. Whois++ was small and quick to install. Netfind gathered data on its own without asking anyone. Archie worked because the files it indexed were already there to be fetched.

sections.title: Problems to Overcome
sections.content:
The report divides the problems into technology issues and infrastructure. On technology, many people suggest that a public domain version of X.500 is necessary before a widespread service can operate. The public domain program, quipu, is said to be difficult to install and to bring into operation, is not quite standard X.500, and is more suited to research than production service. The report notes that many who tried earlier versions abandoned X.500 because of its costly start up time and inherent complexity, and that the ISODE Consortium was developing newer features. The client side needs work too, since X.500 has a sharp learning curve, and access to the directory should be built into other applications such as Gopher and email, especially for accessing PEM X.509 certificates. Data conversion tools are needed to move between systems, and searching needs improvement, including index servers that store information on a few key attributes.

On infrastructure, the key issues are central management and naming rules. X.500 is not run as a service in the United States, so those using it there are not assured of the reliability of root servers. The report says X.500 cannot be taken seriously until there is some central management and coordinated administration support in place, and that someone has to be responsible for maintaining the root, an effort comparable to maintaining the root of the DNS. PSI provided that service until the end of the FOX project. New sites need help in getting their servers up and linked to a central server.

Section 5 sets out the wider issues. On data protection, the report notes that outside the United States nearly all developed countries have strict data protection acts governing databases of personal data, that whoever runs such a database must control what can be stored and retrieved, and that if modification is allowed then authentication is required. On searching, the report points out that a distributed directory cannot search every leaf of the tree in reasonable time, so the search space for any given search must be limited, which makes the directory harder to use. On indexing, the suggestion for fast searching is to pre-compute an index of people across the distributed database and hold it in an index server, so a search first asks the index server, which returns a pointer to the databases that hold matching records. On collection and maintenance, the information must be live, and one approach is to use existing databases, with a defined use of SQL as the standard interface language between those databases and the directory server.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of work stood in the way. The software was hard to install and slow to learn, and nobody was in charge of the top of the system, the way the DNS root is managed. Separately, a directory spread over many servers cannot be searched from end to end, so it needs indexes to narrow the search.

sections.title: Deployment Strategy and Recommendations
sections.content:
The report says no solution will arise simply by providing technical specifications: the solution must fit the way the Internet adopts information technology. The systems that gained real momentum, WAIS and Gopher, followed a model. A small group goes off and builds a piece of software that supplies badly needed functionality at feasible effort. The community rapidly adopts the system as a de facto standard. Many people then join the developers in improving the system and standardising the protocols.

Four recommendations follow. Adopt the common ground approach, giving all protocols equal access to all data, encouraging multiple client and server types and the standardisation of an interoperation protocol between them. The clients may be simple clients, front-ends, gateways, or embedded in other information access clients such as Gopher or WWW client programs, and the interoperation protocol will define message types, message sequences and data fields, with the use of URLs as an element. Promote the development of index servers, which should use several different methods both for gathering data for their indices and for searching them. Support a central management for the X.500 system, because it is essential to provide the relatively small amount of central management necessary to keep the system functioning. And support the development of security certificate storage and retrieval from the white pages service, initially focusing on the existing X.500 directory infrastructure, with work also needed for other services such as Whois++.

The report adds the deployment issues. A strict hierarchical layout is not suitable for all directory applications and should not be forced on them. A typical organisation's hierarchical information is often proprietary, and institutions will always have some information they do not wish to display publicly. There is a problem of multiple directory service providers, and a more general approach using a knowledge server, or a set of servers, might be better. Guidelines are needed for methods of searching and using directory information, and a registration authority is needed to register names at various levels of the hierarchy to ensure uniqueness. On X.500 in the United States, the report notes that the lack of support for building and maintaining infrastructure since the demise of the FOX project is a serious problem, and that without funding X.500 may not stand a chance there. It also notes that the X.500-Gopher gateway has had the greatest impact on providing widespread access, and that since adding X.500 as a service on the ESnet Gopher, the use of the ESnet DSA has risen dramatically.
sections.plainLanguage: Write the software, let people use it, then standardise what grew. The report also says to keep X.500 running properly with someone in charge of its root, to build indexes that make searching fast, and to let different systems talk to each other through a common protocol.

sections.title: The Functionality List
sections.content:
Appendix 1 holds the White Pages Functionality List, developed by Chris Weider and amended by participants in the discussion. It is arranged as requirements for three things: a service that serves information on people only, a yellow pages service with data primarily on people, and advanced directory services for resource location rather than just people data.

The protocol requirements for the people-only service are distributability, security, searchability and easy navigation, reliability in particular replication, the ability to serve the information desired including multi-media information, obvious benefits to encourage installation, protocol support for maintenance of data and knowledge, the ability to support machine use of the data, being based on open standards and responding rapidly to correct deficiencies, serving new types of information only upon request, and allowing different operation modes. The implementation requirements add searchability and easy navigation, a painless upgrade path, obvious benefits to encourage installation, ubiquitous clients, clients that can do exhaustive search or cache useful information and use heuristics to narrow the search space for ill-formed queries, machine use of the data, and stable APIs.

The sociological requirements are a shallow learning curve for novice users on both client and server, public domain servers and clients to encourage experimentation, easy techniques for maintaining data so that users keep it up to date, the ability for an organisation to hide its internal structure while making the data public, widely recognised authorities to guarantee unique naming during registrations, the ability to support the privacy and legal requirements of all participants while still achieving good coverage, and supportable infrastructure.

The Security Considerations section is candid: while the memo contains comments about privacy and security, there is no serious analysis of security considerations for a white pages or directory service in it.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is a checklist of what a directory service must do, split into the protocol, the software and the people. It also says plainly that the report does not analyse security.

viz.caption: THE FOUR RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE MEETING

items.title: Common ground
items.text: Give all protocols equal access to all data through a shared interoperation protocol.

items.title: Index servers
items.text: Build servers that pre-compute indexes so that searches are fast.

items.title: Central management
items.text: Give the X.500 system the small amount of central management it needs to keep working.

items.title: Certificate storage
items.text: Store and retrieve security certificates, first through the existing X.500 infrastructure.
